Golden Girls [6224]

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...we meet the Golden Girls who brought back medals for South Africa in a global athletics competition

Unique Selling Point:
Three South African seniors - aged 60, 70 and 80 - won gold medals in the World Master's Athletics Championships in Finland this year, making up six of the ten gold medals won by the South African team. They are all race-walkers which is a challenging athletics discipline requiring huge concentration and training. Yet they are all amateurs, self-funded and at least one of them is self-taught. This is an inspiring story of older women who have never given up on their own abilities, driven by a competitive spirit which has not withered with time, at a time when the value of age is often eclipsed by the charisma of youth.

Summary:
Each of our Golden Girls has a different story. The seventy-year-old Edna has been race-walking since she was in her fifties. She learnt by watching others and it kept her going through her husband's illness of dementia, which caused his death a few years ago. When she went to Finland this year, she had never travelled overseas before and took a neighbour as her cheerleader and aide-de-camp. To get there she had to crowd-fund in her community. Hildegaard Vey, at 80, is the more experienced of the three. She has been to eight World Masters over two decades and won a clutch of awards - winning a hat-trick of three this year in Finland. She learnt how to race-walk in Johannesburg but since moving to Cape Town with her very supportive husband eight years ago, she has trained on her own. She admits that what keeps her going is her fiercely competitive spirit as well as a disciplined life - only one cup of coffee a day, staying slim and not giving up. Ronelle Botha is the youngest in the group at sixty - she trains with a very good coach in Alberton where she lives, but works during the week at a school/creche. I need to get more information from her about her life. She is being coached by Carl Meyer, one of the unsung legends of South African race-walking who would be a good expert on this sport, which requires a great deal of technique and discipline.

Further information:
Edna Brand is participating in a walk in Kuilsrivier Sat 3rd of September - I am going to film her participating in the race in order to have good walking footage in a competitive environment. One of the shoots will be in Gauteng, and it would be good if Siniketiwe manages it.

Press Release:


The Golden Girls
It's an Olympic sport, not celebrated with much fanfare. But for three South African seniors - aged 60, 70 and 80 – race-walking is an athletics discipline that gives them a continuing zest for life. So much so that each walked away with gold medals at the World Master's Athletics Championships in Finland this year, making up six of the ten gold medals won by the South African team. In an era where the value of age is often eclipsed by the charisma of youth, these women aren’t looking to any fountain to defy time. Carte Blanche took on our gold winning champions.
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli



Script:


GOLDEN GIRLS for Second Viewing Script Friday 16 Sept 2022 pm


(VO) Competitive athletics celebrate the young – but some of South Africa’s unsung heroes are over thirty-five years, and in their age groups, they are of the best in the world.

MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: A relatively small South African squad of 22 athletes entered the World Masters Athletics this year, competing against 4000 other athletes from 86 countries. South Africa claimed 10 gold medals, but six of those were won by the dynamic trio now tagged the Golden Girls.

(VO) South African race-walkers Hildegard Vey, Edna Brand and Ronelle Botha are all 2022 world champions in their discipline – race-walking.

EDNA BRAND: I was praying as I was going along, please Lord, just just keep me strong, let me just go, you know, don’t let me get tired.

MACFARLANE: Does still give you goosebumps when you get onto that podium and you hear the national anthem?
HILDEGARD VEY: Yes
MACFARLANE: How does that feel?
HILDEGARD VEY: It does, it actually brings tears to my eyes. People don't realise how much work goes into it. Cos it’s a lot.

RONELLE BOTHA: It was very unreal, very emotional. I never expected it. And on the day everything went my way.

(VO) At 60 years, Ronelle Botha is the youngest of the trio. She’s a maths teacher - but she finds time to train most days a week.

RONELLE BOTHA: I can’t do without it. I’m absolutely hooked.

(VO) At the Boksburg Stadium track, Ronelle and her coach Carl Meyer warm up. And then he starts with a master class. The rules are strictly observed. At all times, one foot must be on the ground, and the leg must be straight.

CARL MEYER: Shoulders nice and down - ok – it’s just the arms that swing, and now we are going to go forward and there we go!
MACFARLANE: Cool!
CARL MEYER: That’s it! That’s it!
MACFARLANE: Walker!

(VO) Carl is a sought-after coach, he’s been involved in competitive race-walking for half a century, since he was at school.

MACFARLANE: And then as a competitor, how easy is it then also to get disqualified with all of these rules that you talk about?

CARL MEYER: That is exactly the point. You want to participate right on the edge of what is legal. If you are not on that edge, then you haven’t pushed yourself to the, to the limits.

(VO) The fear of being disqualified keeps a competitive race-walker in a state of constant focus.

CARL MEYER: So there's a number of judges around the track. So you come around, you see on the DQ board, you've got three red dots, the you know, well okay, next time you come around, you're gonna go into what they call the sinbin.
MACFARLANE: Shew
CARL MEYER: So there you stand, depending on the distance: 30 seconds for five k, one minute for 10k, two minutes for twenty k and three and a half minutes for 35 ks.
MACFARLANE: Have you ever been in the sinbin?
RONELLE: No
CARL MEYER: No, not
MACFARLANE: You must have a good coach!
CARL MEYER: My athletes hardly ever go to the sinbin.


MACFARLANE: So Ronelle, this is your wall of fame, right?
RONELLE BRAND: Yes.
MACFARLANE: What are all these medals for?
RONELLE: They are mostly the Provincial champs and some SA champs.
MACFARLANE: One’s from Finland, this one, this one over here?
RONELLE: Yes
MACFARLANE: This is your gold.
RONELLE BRAND: Yes. And the podium photo next to it with that very long smile.

( VO) Ronelle won her gold medal for the 20 km race - her seventy-year-old friend Edna Brand took the winning streak further with one silver and two golds

MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Self-taught, self-funded, and self-motivated, Edna Brand has been race-walking since she was in her forties.

EDNA BRAND: I was always practising with the runners. So it sort of forced me also to, to get faster and -
MACFARLANE: To try and keep up?
EDNA BRAND: To try and keep up! And I seem to have that competitive edge because I enjoyed it. So I've always trying to improve and to get faster.

(VO) Edna’ participation in local races keeps her on form and her spirits high. She’s won a treasure trove of medals in this endurance sport.

MACFARLANE: These are like your SA colours?
EDNA BRAND: Ja, these are the SA championships

(VO) But until this year, Edna had never attempted to test her speed on the global track.

EDNA BRAND: I said, Oh my gosh, I've never been overseas. How on earth am I going to do this? This is very scary.
MACFARLANE: So it was your first overseas trip - to Finland?
EDNA BRAND: My first overseas trip as well. So I contacted –
MACFARLANE: So many firsts – unbelievable?
EDNA BRAND: Ja, Ja Absolutely. Life started again at seventy.

MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Initially Edna was not going to attend the World Master’s Athletics because she simply couldn’t afford the cost of flying overseas, but her friends and family rallied around her to make sure she got on to the track.

(VO) Edna’s next door neighbour, Yvonne, offered to be the chaperone – and they set off on a big adventure.

YVONNE BESTER: When I speak about this I want to cry again because I was there for the five, the ten and the twenty kilometres.

Sound up of Yvonne from mobile phone footage:
Hier kom sy, hier kom sy, hier kom my buurvrou, vir twintig kilometers, vir ‘n goue medalje, hier kom sy! Fokus, fokus, fokus, fokus buurvrou focus, fokus!

Translation: Here she comes, here she comes, here comes my neighbour for the twenty kilometres, for a gold medal, here she comes, focus, focus, focus, focus neighbour, focus!

YVONNE BESTER: I was crying, I was taking the photograph but I was shaking so much.

Announcer: Edna Brand, South Africa
Yvonne Bester’s Voice: Wheh, Champion, World Champion!

(VO) There are no professional camera crews to capture these triumphs - but Edna’s family and friends were monitoring her every step on whatsapp - and by the time she got home, she was a hero.

MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Winning gold at sixty is one thing, and then at seventy years old, that’s another.
But clinching not one, not two, but three gold medals as an octogenarian athlete, now that is in another league altogether.

HILDEGARD VEY: I go out every day, every single day except a Wednesday. I do speed work, I do hill work, I do distance. I can get in in 10 Ks, I can work at that. I've been getting 20 getting 18 Ks, if I go down all the side roads.

(VO) Hilde postponed a painful toe operation until after the championships – she has six pins in her feet altogether, and one foot is in a boot. But the veteran athlete is impatient to get back on the road – she has her race routines finely honed.

HILDEGARD VEY: When I do a race, for a 5k hike, I buy goo gums. And I cut them in half. And I stick it where I shouldn't….And I just stick it in, and then I take out - because that's the most convenient place when I'm moving..

(VO) Of the three Golden Girls, Hildegard has the most mileage on the clock, having competed in eight World championships. But in her final 20ks this year, she ended up racing against herself.

HILDEGARD VEY: I was on my own, in an 80. And that’s quite hard for me because I like a carrot. I like – anyway, so I got in and I was doing ok, and then it started to rain. And then it really down-poured when I was doing the last 17 and I can’t race-walk in the water –
MACFARLANE: In the rain?
HILDEGARDE VEY: Yes, and and not only that, I was a little bit reluctant with the falling. At this age, I’ve got to be very careful.

CARL MEYER: The three of them is going to surprise the world further. Edna and Hildegard are stars in their own right, Ronelle has just entered the fray herself now, so each one of them in a different age category. And that is what is making Master’s Athletics so exciting.

HILDEGARDE VEY: I’m very competitive, I'm very competitive.

(VO) But for these champions, it’s not just about the sport or the winning times, it’s also about the deep friendships they’ve made along the way.

RONELLE BRAND: There’s a camaraderie amongst the walkers that I have never found anywhere else.
EDNA BRAND: It was just like we were a little family from you know – together –so it’s nice .

(VO) Walking – winning – and celebrating together – these are South Africa’s Golden Girls.

PROMOS

PROMO 1: - must be 21 seconds

(VO) Aged sixty, seventy and eighty – gold and silver medals for three remarkable athletes
EDNA BRAND: Being on the podium, and then playing your country's anthem. That was such an amazing, amazing feeling.


PROMO 2: : - must be 21 seconds

(VO)The best in the world - these are South Africa’s Golden Girls
HILDEGARD VEY: It actually brings tears to my eyes because people don't realise how much work goes into it. Cos it’s a lot

MACFARLANE: So Ronelle, this is your wall of fame, right? RONELLE BRAND: Yes. MACFARLANE: What are all these medals for? RONELLE: They are mostly the Provincial champs and some SA champs. MACFARLANE: One’s from Finland, this one, this one over here? RONELLE: Yes MACFARLANE: This is your gold. RONELLE BRAND: Yes. And the podium photo next to it with that very long smile. ( VO) Ronelle won her gold medal for the 20 km race - her seventy-year-old friend Edna Brand took the winning streak further with one silver and two golds MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Self-taught, self-funded, and self-motivated, Edna Brand has been race-walking since she was in her forties. EDNA BRAND: I was always practising with the runners. So it sort of forced me also to, to get faster and - MACFARLANE: To try and keep up? EDNA BRAND: To try and keep up! And I seem to have that competitive edge because I enjoyed it. So I've always trying to improve and to get faster. (VO) Edna’ participation in local races keeps her on form and her spirits high. She’s won a treasure trove of medals in this endurance sport. MACFARLANE: These are like your SA colours? EDNA BRAND: Ja, these are the SA championships (VO) But until this year, Edna had never attempted to test her speed on the global track. EDNA BRAND: I said, Oh my gosh, I've never been overseas. How on earth am I going to do this? This is very scary. MACFARLANE: So it was your first overseas trip - to Finland? EDNA BRAND: My first overseas trip as well. So I contacted – MACFARLANE: So many firsts – unbelievable? EDNA BRAND: Ja, Ja Absolutely. Life started again at seventy. MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Initially Edna was not going to attend the World Master’s Athletics because she simply couldn’t afford the cost of flying overseas, but her friends and family rallied around her to make sure she got on to the track. (VO) Edna’s next door neighbour, Yvonne, offered to be the chaperone – and they set off on a big adventure. YVONNE BESTER: When I speak about this I want to cry again because I was there for the five, the ten and the twenty kilometres. Sound up of Yvonne from mobile phone footage: Hier kom sy, hier kom sy, hier kom my buurvrou, vir twintig kilometers, vir ‘n goue medalje, hier kom sy! Fokus, fokus, fokus, fokus buurvrou focus, fokus! Translation: Here she comes, here she comes, here comes my neighbour for the twenty kilometres, for a gold medal, here she comes, focus, focus, focus, focus neighbour, focus! YVONNE BESTER: I was crying, I was taking the photograph but I was shaking so much. Announcer: Edna Brand, South Africa Yvonne Bester’s Voice: Wheh, Champion, World Champion! (VO) There are no professional camera crews to capture these triumphs - but Edna’s family and friends were monitoring her every step on whatsapp - and by the time she got home, she was a hero. MACFARLANE PIECE TO CAMERA: Winning gold at sixty is one thing, and then at seventy years old, that’s another. But clinching not one, not two, but three gold medals as an octogenarian athlete, now that is in another league altogether. HILDEGARD VEY: I go out every day, every single day except a Wednesday. I do speed work, I do hill work, I do distance. I can get in in 10 Ks, I can work at that. I've been getting 20 getting 18 Ks, if I go down all the side roads. (VO) Hilde postponed a painful toe operation until after the championships – she has six pins in her feet altogether, and one foot is in a boot. But the veteran athlete is impatient to get back on the road – she has her race routines finely honed. HILDEGARD VEY: When I do a race, for a 5k hike, I buy goo gums. And I cut them in half. And I stick it where I shouldn't….And I just stick it in, and then I take out - because that's the most convenient place when I'm moving.. (VO) Of the three Golden Girls, Hildegard has the most mileage on the clock, having competed in eight World championships. But in her final 20ks this year, she ended up racing against herself. HILDEGARD VEY: I was on my own, in an 80. And that’s quite hard for me because I like a carrot. I like – anyway, so I got in and I was doing ok, and then it started to rain. And then it really down-poured when I was doing the last 17 and I can’t race-walk in the water – MACFARLANE: In the rain? HILDEGARDE VEY: Yes, and and not only that, I was a little bit reluctant with the falling. At this age, I’ve got to be very careful. CARL MEYER: The three of them is going to surprise the world further. Edna and Hildegard are stars in their own right, Ronelle has just entered the fray herself now, so each one of them in a different age category. And that is what is making Master’s Athletics so exciting. HILDEGARDE VEY: I’m very competitive, I'm very competitive. (VO) But for these champions, it’s not just about the sport or the winning times, it’s also about the deep friendships they’ve made along the way. RONELLE BRAND: There’s a camaraderie amongst the walkers that I have never found anywhere else. EDNA BRAND: It was just like we were a little family from you know – together –so it’s nice . (VO) Walking – winning – and celebrating together – these are South Africa’s Golden Girls. PROMOS PROMO 1: - must be 21 seconds (VO) Aged sixty, seventy and eighty – gold and silver medals for three remarkable athletes EDNA BRAND: Being on the podium, and then playing your country's anthem. That was such an amazing, amazing feeling. PROMO 2: : - must be 21 seconds (VO)The best in the world - these are South Africa’s Golden Girls HILDEGARD VEY: It actually brings tears to my eyes because people don't realise how much work goes into it. Cos it’s a lot PROMO 3:must be 11 seconds EDNA BRAND: I was praying as I was going along, please Lord, just just keep me strong,

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ...we meet the Golden Girls who brought back medals for South Africa in a global athletics competition
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Three South African seniors - aged 60, 70 and 80 - won gold medals in the World Master's Athletics Championships in Finland this year, making up six of the ten gold medals won by the South African team. They are all race-walkers which is a challenging athletics discipline requiring huge concentration and training. Yet they are all amateurs, self-funded and at least one of them is self-taught. This is an inspiring story of older women who have never given up on their own abilities, driven by a competitive spirit which has not withered with time, at a time when the value of age is often eclipsed by the charisma of youth.
metadata.Summary: Each of our Golden Girls has a different story. The seventy-year-old Edna has been race-walking since she was in her fifties. She learnt by watching others and it kept her going through her husband's illness of dementia, which caused his death a few years ago. When she went to Finland this year, she had never travelled overseas before and took a neighbour as her cheerleader and aide-de-camp. To get there she had to crowd-fund in her community. Hildegaard Vey, at 80, is the more experienced of the three. She has been to eight World Masters over two decades and won a clutch of awards - winning a hat-trick of three this year in Finland. She learnt how to race-walk in Johannesburg but since moving to Cape Town with her very supportive husband eight years ago, she has trained on her own. She admits that what keeps her going is her fiercely competitive spirit as well as a disciplined life - only one cup of coffee a day, staying slim and not giving up. Ronelle Botha is the youngest in the group at sixty - she trains with a very good coach in Alberton where she lives, but works during the week at a school/creche. I need to get more information from her about her life. She is being coached by Carl Meyer, one of the unsung legends of South African race-walking who would be a good expert on this sport, which requires a great deal of technique and discipline.
metadata.Further information: Edna Brand is participating in a walk in Kuilsrivier Sat 3rd of September - I am going to film her participating in the race in order to have good walking footage in a competitive environment. One of the shoots will be in Gauteng, and it would be good if Siniketiwe manages it.
